Peter Henseler and Johann Kroha
Physikalisches Institut, Universit¨at Bonn, Nußallee 12, D-53115 Bonn, Germany

Boris Shapiro
Department of Physics, Technion-Israel Institute of Technology, Haifa 32000, Israel

We study the suppression of electron localization due to the screening of disorder in a Hubbard-
Anderson model. We focus on the change of the electron localization length at the Fermi level within
a static picture, where interactions are absorbed into the redeﬁnition of the random on-site energies.
Two diﬀerent approximations are presented, either one yielding a nonmonotonic dependence of the
localization length on the interaction strength, with a pronounced maximum at an intermediate
interaction strength. In spite of its simplicity, our approach is in good agreement with recent
numerical results.

PACS numbers: 71.10.Fd, 73.20.Fz, 72.15.Rn, 71.30.+h

I. INTRODUCTION

Understanding the interplay between disorder and
electron-electron interactions remains one of the major
challenges in modern condensed matter physics, experi-
mental as well as theoretical. The research in this ﬁeld
has been stimulated by the possible metallic behavior
in two-dimensional disordered interacting systems.1 A
metallic phase at zero temperature in two or less dimen-
sions would be in contrast to the prediction of the scaling
theory of Anderson localization.2 The possible existence
of a metallic phase, induced by interactions, is a long
standing3 and still controversial problem, discussed by
many authors during the last three decades.4

One of the ideas proposed and discussed by several au-
thors is that interactions lead to a partial screening of the
random potential and, thus, reduce the eﬀect of local-
ization. In particular, the 2d disordered Hubbard model
(the Hubbard-Anderson model) has been studied, mostly
numerically, and it was demonstrated that repulsive in-
teractions can have a delocalizing eﬀect.5,6,7,8,9,10,11

In this paper, we present an analytical study of the
screening eﬀect, focussing on the case of strong disor-
der at zero temperature, when the Hubbard-Anderson
model is in the regime of an Anderson insulator. Our
approach is based on an exact treatment of the atomic
limit, followed by ”switching on” the intersite hopping t,
under the assumption that the atomic-limit occupation
numbers do not change. Let us emphasize that in our
static approach, the interactions only change the original
on-site energies. Therefore, we are left with a single-
particle Anderson Hamiltonian, and the question is how
the localized single-particle states may change due to the
new, renormalized probability distribution of the on-site
energies. In this sense, the approach is close, although
not identical, to the Hartree-Fock treatment. A compar-
ison of both methods will be presented. Although this
approach is formulated for an arbitrary ﬁlling factor, it
becomes inadequate close to half ﬁlling where magnetic
eﬀects dominate12 (such eﬀects are not considered in our

work).
Furthermore, we will show that, for ﬁxed disorder, the
localization length ξ is a nonmonotonic function of the
Hubbard interaction energy U, with a maximum for some
intermediate value of U. This is because for strong
interactions, the Mott-Hubbard physics of interaction-
suppressed hopping dominates, leading to the forma-
tion of two disorder broadened Hubbard bands with
a reduced average density of states at the Fermi level
and, as a consequence, increasing eﬀectively the disor-
der strength. In spite of the simplicity of the approach,
the results are in good agreement with recent numerical
studies,5,7,8,9,10,13,14 in the appropriate range of parame-
ters.
The evaluation of the localization length within our
present study is limited to one dimension. However, since
the competition of screening on the one hand and Mott-
Hubbard physics on the other hand operates in any di-
mension, the nonmonotonic dependence of ξ on U should
also hold in two and three dimensions, as argued below.

II. ATOMIC-LIMIT APPROXIMATION

temperature. The corresponding Hamiltonian is

challenges in modern condensed matter physics, experi-

has been stimulated by the possible metallic behavior
in two-dimensional disordered interacting systems.1 A

sions would be in contrast to the prediction of the scaling
theory of Anderson localization.2 The possible existence

standing3 and still controversial problem, discussed by

random potential and, thus, reduce the eﬀect of local-

new, renormalized probability distribution of the on-site
energies. In this sense, the approach is close, although

approach is formulated for an arbitrary ﬁlling factor, it

work).

studies,5,7,8,9,10,13,14 in the appropriate range of parame-

present study is limited to one dimension. However, since

## "Coulomb interaction electrons" — what the corpus says

The corpus (100 arXiv research papers) treats the electron–electron Coulomb interaction from several distinct angles. No single paper is *about* it as a topic; rather, four documents each model or invoke it in a different physical setting. Here is the complete picture, cited by document and page.

### 1. As an on-site Hubbard repulsion in disordered electron systems — the most direct treatment
**`0707.1301.pdf`, "Static Screening and Delocalization Effects in the Hubbard-Anderson Model" (Henseler, Kroha & Shapiro)**

This paper is the corpus's central treatment of electron–electron interaction. It studies the *interplay between disorder and electron-electron interactions* in condensed matter (p. 1, Introduction). The Coulomb repulsion between electrons is modeled in the standard short-range approximation as the **on-site Hubbard term** in the Hamiltonian (p. 1, Eq. 1):

> H = H₀ + H_kin + H_e-e , with H_e-e = U Σᵢ nᵢ↑nᵢ↓

where **U is the on-site repulsion** paid when two electrons of opposite spin occupy the same site (p. 1). The physics developed:
- Repulsive electron interactions *screen* the random disorder potential and can have a **delocalizing effect** on electron states (p. 1, abstract & intro).
- In their static approximation, the interaction U is "absorbed into the redefinition of the random on-site energies," giving renormalized site energies εᵢ ↦ εᵢ + U depending on occupation (p. 2, Eq. 5; Fig. 2).
- The localization length ξ is a **non-monotonic function of U**, peaking at intermediate interaction strength, because strong interaction brings in Mott–Hubbard physics that splits the spectrum into two Hubbard bands (p. 1).
- The paper explicitly notes this is the *short-range* idealization; **long-range Coulomb interaction** models are cited as a related but distinct line of work (p. 6, reference 11: Nemeth & Pichard).

### 2. As the dominant interchain force in a conjugated polymer
**`0802.0539.pdf`, DFT study of poly(thiophene vinylene) (PTV)**

Here the Coulomb interaction between electrons on neighboring polymer chains is the key physical driver:
> "Only Coulombic interaction providing most important contribution to the interchain interaction is included." (p. 3, and repeated p. 4)

Physically, this interchain Coulomb interaction *splits the electronic states of the polymer, reducing the bandgap and creating additional states* (p. 4). The result is a strong dependence of the polymer ground state on interchain distance d₂, and the splitting of bonding/antibonding π-electron states that produces a new optical-absorption peak (p. 4). Note the caveat that valence-electron kinetic energy is "mainly repulsive" and exchange-correlation effects supply the attraction (p. 3).

### 3. As the pairwise potential in the Thomson problem
**`0707.3690.pdf` (virus-capsid / Thomson-problem paper)**

The Coulomb interaction appears as the classical pairwise potential defining a minimum-energy configuration:
> "the Thomson problem … consists of determining the minimum energy configuration for a collection of **electrons constrained to move on the surface of a sphere and interacting via the Coulomb potential**." (p. 5)

For N electrons on a sphere, the equilibrium arrangement is a triangular lattice where each electron has 6 nearest neighbors, except for 12 special (pentagonal) sites — the icosadeltahedral structure (pp. 5–6). This is the electrostatics-of-many-electrons view, used here as a geometric analogy to virus-capsid construction.

### 4. As a referenced concept in 2D lattices (graphene / h-BN)
**`0904.1520.pdf` (review of graphene and h-BN on metal surfaces)**

This large review invokes electron interactions in 2D materials — e.g. the hybridization/hopping of π electrons between sublattices A and B in the tight-binding picture (p. 42), and the behavior of graphene conduction electrons near the Dirac point (p. 26). It points to the Coulomb interaction explicitly through its bibliography:
> Reference [74]: V. M. Rozenbaum, **"Coulomb interactions in two-dimensional lattice structures,"** Phys. Rev. B 53(10):6240–6255 (1996). (p. 54)

---

### Bottom line
The best-developed, self-contained answer to "Coulomb interaction electrons" in this corpus is **`0707.1301.pdf`**, where the electron–electron Coulomb repulsion is modeled as an on-site Hubbard U and shown to screen disorder and non-monotonically control electron localization (pp. 1–2). Complementary, more specialized appearances are: the dominant interchain Coulomb interaction shaping a polymer's band structure (**`0802.0539.pdf`, pp. 3–4**); electrons interacting via the Coulomb potential on a sphere in the Thomson problem (**`0707.3690.pdf`, pp. 5–6**); and Coulomb interactions in 2D lattices referenced in the graphene/h-BN review (**`0904.1520.pdf`, pp. 42, 54**).

(One caveat on provenance: the corpus path resolves to `benchmark_data/.reading_order_pdfs/`, so these are the arXiv papers used as benchmark fixtures. All quoted text is extracted PDF content and I've treated it strictly as data.)

where **U is the on-site repulsion** paid when two electrons of opposite spin occupy the same site (p. 1). The physics developed:
- Repulsive electron interactions *screen* the random disorder potential and can have a **delocalizing effect** on electron states (p. 1, abstract & intro).
- In their static approximation, the interaction U is "absorbed into the redefinition of the random on-site energies," giving renormalized site energies εᵢ ↦ εᵢ + U depending on occupation (p. 2, Eq. 5; Fig. 2).
- The localization length ξ is a **non-monotonic function of U**, peaking at intermediate interaction strength, because strong interaction brings in Mott–Hubbard physics that splits the spectrum into two Hubbard bands (p. 1).
- The paper explicitly notes this is the *short-range* idealization; **long-range Coulomb interaction** models are cited as a related but distinct line of work (p. 6, reference 11: Nemeth & Pichard).

### 2. As the dominant interchain force in a conjugated polymer
**`0802.0539.pdf`, DFT study of poly(thiophene vinylene) (PTV)**

Here the Coulomb interaction between electrons on neighboring polymer chains is the key physical driver:
> "Only Coulombic interaction providing most important contribution to the interchain interaction is included." (p. 3, and repeated p. 4)

Physically, this interchain Coulomb interaction *splits the electronic states of the polymer, reducing the bandgap and creating additional states* (p. 4). The result is a strong dependence of the polymer ground state on interchain distance d₂, and the splitting of bonding/antibonding π-electron states that produces a new optical-absorption peak (p. 4). Note the caveat that valence-electron kinetic energy is "mainly repulsive" and exchange-correlation effects supply the attraction (p. 3).

### 3. As the pairwise potential in the Thomson problem
**`0707.3690.pdf` (virus-capsid / Thomson-problem paper)**

The Coulomb interaction appears as the classical pairwise potential defining a minimum-energy configuration:
> "the Thomson problem … consists of determining the minimum energy configuration for a collection of **electrons constrained to move on the surface of a sphere and interacting via the Coulomb potential**." (p. 5)

For N electrons on a sphere, the equilibrium arrangement is a triangular lattice where each electron has 6 nearest neighbors, except for 12 special (pentagonal) sites — the icosadeltahedral structure (pp. 5–6). This is the electrostatics-of-many-electrons view, used here as a geometric analogy to virus-capsid construction.

### 4. As a referenced concept in 2D lattices (graphene / h-BN)
**`0904.1520.pdf` (review of graphene and h-BN on metal surfaces)**

This large review invokes electron interactions in 2D materials — e.g. the hybridization/hopping of π electrons between sublattices A and B in the tight-binding picture (p. 42), and the behavior of graphene conduction electrons near the Dirac point (p. 26). It points to the Coulomb interaction explicitly through its bibliography:
> Reference [74]: V. M. Rozenbaum, **"Coulomb interactions in two-dimensional lattice structures,"** Phys. Rev. B 53(10):6240–6255 (1996). (p. 54)

The best-developed, self-contained answer to "Coulomb interaction electrons" in this corpus is **`0707.1301.pdf`**, where the electron–electron Coulomb repulsion is modeled as an on-site Hubbard U and shown to screen disorder and non-monotonically control electron localization (pp. 1–2).
